adv_region_vs_batch.description: LAMP-LED defect batch sold mostly in LATAM, so LATAM (and the home category) look guilty

adv_volume_segment.description: Web carries 65% of volume and the most refunds at a normal rate; CASE-PRO is the real defect

adv_two_factors.description: Two independent causes: BlueDart-Intl non-delivery and a MUG-CLASSIC defect

adv_indistinguishable.description: Every TEE-ORG order ships with ParcelOne and vice versa: partner and SKU cannot be separated

adv_low_sample.description: SwiftShip-EU spike plus a 5-order kiosk channel with an eye-catching refund rate

adv_no_anomaly.description: Normal day; any named driver is a false attribution

data: frozen synthetic scenarios (origin=SYNTHETIC) in the payops_eval database; no PayPal calls

finding.hypothesis: Fulfillment partner NorthPost is failing to deliver orders. That produces a wave of ITEM_NOT_RECEIVED refunds, which drives the overall refund-rate spike.
finding.uncertainty: The tool budget ran out before I could cross-slice NorthPost by region or SKU, or look at individual transactions, so region or category effects can't be fully separated from NorthPost. I also didn't check carrier tracking data. A high refund rate alone does not justify issuing refunds.

finding.hypothesis: Product SKU LAMP-LED (home category) has a defect, and DEFECTIVE refunds on it account for almost all of the refund-rate spike.
finding.uncertainty: I did not cross LAMP-LED with fulfillment partner or channel, so a partner-specific batch problem is still possible. LATAM's share is above 0.25, so the server rule will mark it UNRESOLVED rather than ruled out. The case for confounding rests on the cross-slice in Q7. I checked no individual transactions or batch/lot data.

finding.hypothesis: Most of the refund spike comes from one product, CASE-PRO, whose refunds are all coded DEFECTIVE. The spikes seen by partner, region, channel and category follow from where CASE-PRO is sold and shipped.
finding.uncertainty: Several slices explain more than 0.25 of the excess, so the server's rule cannot confirm they are only confounded: SwiftShip-EU, NorthPost, EU, web, marketplace and electronics. I'm treating them as confounded because the CASE-PRO by partner breakdown shows a high rate with every partner, but I did not run CASE-PRO by region or by channel. I'm assuming CASE-PRO belongs to electronics; I didn't verify this directly. I checked no individual transactions or PayPal records, so I can't rule out refund abuse or a single defective production batch.

finding.hypothesis: There are two separate causes. The main one is SKU MUG-CLASSIC, which has a high refund rate with every fulfillment partner. The second is fulfillment partner BlueDart-Intl, which has high refund rates on non-mug SKUs too.
finding.uncertainty: I ran out of tool calls before checking refund reason codes, so I can't say whether the mug refunds are for damage or defects, or whether BlueDart-Intl's are for non-delivery. The two causes overlap on 37 captures, so their shares add up to more than 1. I didn't cross-slice region or channel, so I can't fully rule them out as confounders. I didn't look at any individual transactions.

finding.hypothesis: Delivery failures at fulfillment partner ParcelOne, which ships only SKU TEE-ORG, explain almost all of the refund spike.
finding.uncertainty: The investigation cannot fully separate the shipping partner from the SKU, because every ParcelOne order is TEE-ORG. I chose the partner as the cause because of the ITEM_NOT_RECEIVED reason, but the data cannot rule out a TEE-ORG-specific problem. The TEE-ORG, apparel, NA and mobile slices each explain more than 25% of the excess, so ruling them out cannot be confirmed by the server's 0.25 rule and will show as unresolved. Region and channel were not cross-sliced against ParcelOne. No individual transactions were checked against PayPal.

finding.hypothesis: Fulfillment partner NorthPost is a suspected contributing factor in the refund spike, consistent with delivery failures (ITEM_NOT_RECEIVED).
finding.uncertainty: This is an association that survived stratification, not proven causation; carrier and tracking data are needed to confirm. LATAM and LAMP-LED outside NorthPost had too little data to rule out small independent effects. Other elevated slices (APAC, TEE-ORG, CASE-PRO, electronics/home/apparel) were not tested directly, though NorthPost's lift held within every region, SKU and category and only 8 refunds fell outside NorthPost. No transaction-level or buyer-memo review was done.

finding.hypothesis: SKU LAMP-LED is a suspected contributing factor behind the refund spike. Every one of its refunds is coded DEFECTIVE, which suggests a product quality or batch problem.
finding.uncertainty: The test shows an association that survives stratification, not proven causation. The DEFECTIVE reason codes have not been checked against inspections of returned units. Individual transactions and buyer memos were not reviewed, so possible refund abuse has not been ruled out. Fulfillment partners were not tested directly.

finding.hypothesis: The refund spike is concentrated in SKU CASE-PRO, with refunds coded DEFECTIVE. This points to a product quality or defect problem rather than a partner, region or channel problem. CASE-PRO is a suspected contributing factor, not a proven root cause.
finding.uncertainty: This is a statistical association, not proven causation. A defective batch or a listing or spec mismatch for CASE-PRO is plausible, but it has not been confirmed. Once CASE-PRO is excluded, the remaining slices are too small (fewer than 5 refunds) to rule out a minor second driver. No transaction-level or PayPal records were checked, because the tool budget ran out.

finding.hypothesis: MUG-CLASSIC is the suspected main contributing factor, and BlueDart-Intl is a second, independent suspected contributing factor.
finding.uncertainty: These are associations that held up under stratification, not proven causes. I didn't look up the refund reasons for BlueDart-Intl or check individual transactions, and I didn't run test_hypothesis on home or any region. The SKU's defect explanation rests only on reason-code counts.

finding.hypothesis: The spike is concentrated in one group of 130 captures that are both fulfillment_partner=ParcelOne and product_sku=TEE-ORG (apparel). The data cannot say which of the two is responsible.
finding.uncertainty: fulfillment_partner=ParcelOne and product_sku=TEE-ORG cover exactly the same captures, so they cannot be told apart. A shipping problem at ParcelOne and a problem with the TEE-ORG product are both possible. The ITEM_NOT_RECEIVED reasons point toward shipping but do not prove it. I could not re-check for a hidden second driver because no driver was confirmed to exclude.

finding.hypothesis: Fulfillment partner SwiftShip-EU is the suspected contributing factor: its orders are being refunded mostly as ITEM_NOT_RECEIVED.
finding.uncertainty: This shows a statistical association that held up under stratification, not proven causation. I did not check carrier tracking data or any individual transactions. Kiosk (5 captures) is too small to assess. A second minor driver in very small slices cannot be fully ruled out.

finding.hypothesis: No refund spike is present. The overall refund rate is below baseline, and no segment has enough refunds to support a suspected contributing factor.
finding.uncertainty: With only 8 refunds in the window, the tests cannot detect any segment-level effect. SwiftShip-EU has the largest difference vs the rest of traffic (z 1.85), but the data cannot tell a real partner problem apart from random noise, and cannot separate it from EU, which may overlap with it. None of the z-scores vs a segment's own baseline is meaningful.

finding.hypothesis: Most likely, SwiftShip-EU is failing to deliver orders, and customers are getting refunds for items they never received.
finding.uncertainty: Category (electronics 0.4245, home 0.4205) and channel (web 0.3709, marketplace 0.3529) also pass the 0.25 share threshold. I'm treating them as side effects of the SwiftShip-EU problem, not separate causes. Q8 supports this for category, but I could not cross-check channel or region against the partner because the tool budget ran out. I also did not review any individual transactions or carrier tracking data.

finding.hypothesis: No refund spike exists in this window. The refund rate is below baseline, and every dimension's excess is under 2 refunds.
finding.uncertainty: The sample is small (240 captures, 8 refunds). SwiftShip-EU (7.27% vs 4.91% baseline) and MUG-CLASSIC (4.88% vs 2.65%) are slightly elevated but based on very few refunds. They can't be confirmed or ruled out with this data. Refund reasons and individual transactions were not examined.
